title: More or less: pick one of three pricing strategies and commit to its consequences
summary: Jason Cohen argues there are three viable pricing strategies: more for more, more for less, and less for less. Each carries consequences for product, marketing, hiring and funding that must be accepted together. The only wrong move is not choosing, which leaves a confusing message and a product that's right for no one.

principles.text: Pick one of three pricing strategies and accept its full batch of consequences, or you get a Frankenstein product.
principles.quote: You must pick one approach, and accept its batch of consequences. If you don't incorporate those consequences into the rest of your strategy, you'll have a confusing market message, a Frankenstein product, and the wrong pricing model.

principles.text: Being 'the best' means being best at something specific, and customers must agree it's worth the higher price.
principles.quote: So, the first question is: The best at what? It could be anything, but it has to be specific, and customers have to agree it's worth the higher price tag.

principles.text: Founders wrongly assume 'I built it for myself' means others will pay; use your spark as a starting point, then interview customers.
principles.quote: They think that just because *they* love it, and they "built it for myself" and therefore "I am the customer," and therefore other people will also to pay to solve that problem, in that way. They rarely do.

principles.text: More for less wins most customers, revenue and profit; treat it as its own strategy, not a compromise between best and cheapest.
principles.quote: it is in fact the "More for less" category that wins most of the customers and most of the revenue and most of the profits.

principles.text: Target an ideal customer for whom you're the best; leniency elsewhere means you still win many more customers than you expect.
principles.quote: For your ideal customer, you are in fact "the best," and they cannot believe they're getting the "More for more" product for the "More for less" price.

principles.text: On a more-for-less price, only build features used by at least half of customers or that 15% buy you for.
principles.quote: build only those features used by at least 50% of customers, or where at least 15% of customers buy you specifically for that reason.
